questions.q: Why is 'little attention being paid to the trial'?
choices: Rich new gold has been discovered at Odendaalsrust in the Orange Free State
questions.explain: Men prophesy 'a new Johannesburg will rise there.'

questions.q: How do men at the Stock Exchange behave when the news breaks?
choices: They 'go mad' — shouting, screaming, throwing their hats in the air as shares climb
They sell everything and go home
questions.explain: The 'wonder-share of Tweede Vlei' rises from twenty shillings toward a hundred.

questions.q: What alternative uses for the money do the welfare workers and Father Beresford suggest — before being dismissed as 'muddled'?
choices: Anti-erosion works, boys' and girls' clubs, social centres, more hospitals, and higher pay for the miners
questions.explain: Most of them, it is admitted, 'haven't one share-certificate to rub against another.'

questions.q: What does Sir Ernest Oppenheimer say about the new gold field?
choices: That it 'need not be so' — here is a chance to try settled mine labour, in villages not compounds, where a man can live with his wife and children
questions.explain: There is also talk the Government may set up something like the Tennessee Valley Authority to control the area.

questions.q: What refrain does the narrator repeat about money and the mines?
choices: 'For mines are for men, not for money' — money is for food, clothes, comfort, security and dreams
questions.explain: 'Money is for buying the fruits of the earth, of the land where you were born.'

choices: 'No second Johannesburg is needed upon the earth. One is enough.'
With rain falling on the Free State
questions.explain: The line rejects the giddy dream of repeating Johannesburg's mistakes.

questions.q: How is the site of the new gold field described before the drilling?
choices: Flat rolling veld — sheep, cattle, native herd-boys, grass and bushes, a field of maize here and there
questions.explain: The only watchers are a passing herd-boy or an old Afrikaans-speaking farmer on his horse.

choices: An obscure weekly pamphlet brought out by the missionary Father Beresford
questions.explain: The 'Kafferboeties' and welfare workers write mostly for such small publications.

questions.q: What is the tone of this chapter?
choices: Bitter satire — mocking the market frenzy and the excuses made for not spending the wealth on the poor
questions.explain: 'A man must get something for his courage and foresight, and there's mental strain too.'

questions.q: According to the satirical logic of the chapter, why does the price of shares have 'nothing to do with' miners' wages?
choices: Because wages are fixed by law
Because wages are said to be 'determined solely by mining costs and the price of gold' — so the windfall 'muddled' thinkers want spent on wages is treated as separate
Because the miners own shares too
Because there is no connection worth discussing
questions.explain: The narrator lets the self-serving argument condemn itself.
